# CrSBr: expert Raman notes

Numbers are as printed in the cited source unless marked "(fig)" (read from a plot, about +-1 cm-1). Locators
"p." for arXiv PDFs are arXiv page numbers; "corpus p." are page numbers of the group Lit-RAG PDF copy.
Not used here by design: Wdowik et al. 2025 (arXiv 2503.15298) and Sahu et al. 2025 (arXiv 2502.01794), which sit
behind held-out evaluation data.

## Structure, magnetism, irreps
- Orthorhombic Pmmn (D2h), 6 atoms per primitive cell, 15 optical + 3 acoustic modes (Pawbake et al. 2023, PRB 107,
  075421, arXiv 2211.12939, p.3). Gamma = 3Ag + 2B1u + 3B2g + 2B2u + 3B3g + 2B3u; Ag, B2g, B3g Raman active
  (Torres et al. 2022, arXiv 2212.01754, p.2, Eq. 1).
- In normal-incidence backscattering (light along c) only the three Ag modes are expected; B2g and B3g have
  off-diagonal xz / yz tensors and stay weak (Torres 2022, p.2, Eq. 2; consensus).
- Magnetism: intralayer FM with spins along b (easy axis), A-type interlayer AFM below T_N; intermediate phase (iFM)
  between T_N and T_C (Pawbake 2023, p.1). Reported values differ slightly by source: T_C = 160 K, T_N = 134 K
  (Torres 2022, p.8); T_C about 165 K, T_N about 132 K (Markina et al. 2026, npj Quantum Mater. 11, 11,
  doi:10.1038/s41535-026-00850-2, corpus p.3). A low-temperature phase near T* about 40 K is DISPUTED: reported by
  Pawbake 2023 (p.2, p.4) and others, absent in high-quality crystals per Uykur et al. 2024 (arXiv 2405.07853, p.1).
- Easy (b), intermediate (a) and hard (c) axes; exfoliated flakes are rectangular with the long edge along a
  (Mondal et al. 2025, npj 2D Mater., arXiv 2410.22164, p.1; Torres 2022, p.2).

## Signature at room temperature
- Ag1, Ag2, Ag3: 114, 244, 344 cm-1 (4L, 2.33 and 1.96 eV, Mondal 2025, p.2); 117, 257, 345 cm-1 (bulk, 633 nm,
  Pawbake 2023, p.3); 115, 245.5, 344 cm-1 (bulk, 2.33 eV, Klein et al. 2023, ACS Nano 17, 5316,
  doi:10.1021/acsnano.2c07316, corpus p.5, Fig. 3). Note the Ag2 spread (244 to 257) between sources; treat Ag2
  position with the source's calibration in mind.
- B2g at 92, 194, 301 cm-1 appear only with the sample tilted 60 deg to the beam (Pawbake 2023, p.3, Fig. 1c).
- Atomic character: Ag1 and Ag2 carry Br motion and mediate interlayer coupling; Ag3 is mostly intralayer
  (Torres 2022, p.2, Fig. 1e).

## Thickness
- Ag1 and Ag2 redshift as layer number decreases, Ag3 is nearly layer independent (Torres 2022, p.3, Fig. 1h,
  resonant 1.58 eV). From Fig. 1h (fig): Ag1 about 107 cm-1 in 1L versus about 113 in bulk; Ag3 near 344 for all N.
  Ye et al. 2022 (ACS Nano 16, 11876, doi:10.1021/acsnano.2c01151, corpus p.6) also report a gradual downshift with
  decreasing N. Consensus on direction; exact per-layer values vary with laser and substrate.
- Polarization behaviour of all three Ag modes is the same from about 3.5 to 62 nm (Mondal 2025, p.4-5, Fig. 4);
  for thick flakes (62 nm) thin-film interference changes the Ag2/Ag3 intensity ratio (Mondal 2025, p.4-5).
- Layer number is better taken from optical contrast or AFM than from Raman shifts (Ye 2022, corpus p.5).

## Polarization relative to crystal axes
- Ag1 and Ag3 are maximal for E parallel to b at all tested energies (1.96 to 2.33 eV) (Mondal 2025, p.3-4).
- Ag2 switches by 90 deg with laser energy: maximal along a at 2.33 and 2.25 eV, near isotropic at 2.06 eV, along b
  at 1.96 eV, back along a at 1.58 eV (Mondal 2025, p.3-4, Fig. 3; Klein 2023, corpus p.5, Fig. 3d-f).
- Fits need a complex Raman tensor (relative phase phi_ab between R_xx and R_yy), otherwise four-lobed Ag2 patterns
  (2.25 eV) cannot be reproduced (Mondal 2025, p.6, Eq. 2).
- PL at 1.31 eV (300 K) is stronger along b; it is an independent axis check (Mondal 2025, p.2, Fig. 1d-e).

## Excitation energy and lineshape
- Near-gap excitation (1.58 eV) gives non-Lorentzian Ag modes, extra resonant peaks polarized along b, and a Fano
  (BWF) Ag2 for E parallel to b with 1/q = -0.24; along a Ag2 is Lorentzian (Klein 2023, corpus p.5-6; Torres 2022,
  p.3, Fig. 1f).
- Second-order bands (370 to 780 cm-1, widths 20 to 30 cm-1) appear below about 160 K with 1.96 eV excitation,
  growing on cooling; attributed partly to resonance with the B exciton at 1.82 eV (Pawbake 2023, p.5, Fig. 5).

## Temperature and magnetic order
- Ag3 hardens on cooling, is nearly flat between T_C and T_N, hardens again, then jumps at about 25 K; its FWHM
  shows an inflection near 140 K (Pawbake 2023, p.4, Fig. 3; bulk, 633 nm).
- Intensities of most modes rise in the iFM window 130 to 160 K (Pawbake 2023, p.4).
- Zone folding along c below T_N: a B3g mode at 57 cm-1 (Z point) appears below about 130 K while the 71 cm-1 B3g
  (Gamma, seen below 260 K) disappears; a mode near 194 cm-1 grows near T_C; tilted geometry needed (Pawbake 2023,
  p.4-5, Fig. 4a).
- Sharp 467 cm-1 peak (FWHM 2 cm-1) only below about 40 K, origin unresolved (Pawbake 2023, p.5).
- Thin flakes (3L, 1.58 eV): Ag1 intensity rises strongly below T_C and saturates at T_N; frequencies stay constant
  below T_N, unlike anharmonic behaviour (Torres 2022, p.8).
- Polarization b/a ratios change near T_N under 1.96 eV for 5 to 76 nm flakes (Ag1 step-like); the authors argue the
  spin-phonon effect is indirect, via exciton resonances (Markina 2026, corpus p.4, p.6, Fig. 2). Interpretation
  not yet independently confirmed.
- Infrared (not Raman): a magnetic mode near 360 cm-1 below T_N and splitting of the 180 cm-1 a-axis phonon
  (Uykur 2024, arXiv 2405.07853, p.3-4). Do not assign a 360 cm-1 Raman feature to it without polarization and T data.

## Magnetic field
- Bulk, 5 K, field 30 deg from c: the 57 cm-1 AFM mode fades and the 71 cm-1 mode returns above about 0.8 T, and
  B2g near 305 cm-1 gains intensity; saturation field from magneto-PL 0.75 T in that geometry (Pawbake 2023, p.5,
  Fig. 4b-d). The critical field depends on field direction and layer number (odd/even effect, Ye 2022, corpus p.11,
  Fig. 3).

## Defects, degradation, quality
- D1: shoulder 5 to 10 cm-1 below Ag1, surface related, grows with air or water exposure, strongest in thin flakes

## Calibration and spectral accuracy
- A first-order (linear) pixel-to-wavelength calibration of a single-grating spectrograph gave Raman shift
  errors of 5.0 to -6.8 cm-1 across the detector; with only 3 Hg lines, up to 18 cm-1; adding the quadratic
  term brought it within +-0.3 cm-1 (Lee et al. 2012, Nat. Commun. 3, 1024; arXiv 1209.0234, Methods p.10).
  Their check: graphite G 1581.5 +- 0.3 cm-1 over 12 spots.
- The error depends on where on the detector a line falls, so a single Si-line check near 520 cm-1 does not
  validate a 2D band near 2700 cm-1 [inference from the same mechanism].
- Si first order is quoted as 520 (Lee et al. 2010, ACS Nano 4, 2695; arXiv 1005.2509) and 520.9 cm-1
  (Castellanos-Gomez et al. 2014, arXiv 1403.0499, p.7) in different setups: small offsets between labs are
  normal, so compare shifts relative to an internal reference measured in the same session.

## Resolution, grating and instrument line shape
- Measure resolution from the Rayleigh line: 1.9 vs 9.4 cm-1 on two instruments in one study; spectra then fit
  with Voigt profiles and the Lorentzian FWHM taken as the lifetime width (Das et al. 2008, Nat. Nanotechnol.
  3, 210; arXiv 0709.1174, p.2). About 0.6 cm-1 with a triple-filter low-frequency setup (Zhang et al. 2013,
  PRB 87, 115413; arXiv 1212.6796, p.2); 2.7 cm-1 in Lee 2010 (docs/verified-reference-numbers.md).
- Widths near the resolution (hBN 3 to 9 cm-1, BP Ag2 3 to 7 cm-1; see material notes) are instrument-limited:
  never compare raw FWHM across setups without the resolution. A 0.5 cm-1 resolution was not enough to count BP
  layers from positions (Castellanos-Gomez 2014, p.8).

## Laser heating, power density and photodamage
- Do a power series: Ferrari et al. 2006 saw no change from about 4 to 0.04 mW at 100x (arXiv
  cond-mat/0606284, p.2); typical working powers 1 mW with about 1 um spot (Cancado et al. 2011, arXiv
  1105.0175, p.2), 0.23 mW (Zhang 2013, p.2), below 300 uW at 0.5 NA (Janzen et al. 2023, arXiv 2306.13358,
  p.7). Quote power density, not power: the same mW gives different heating at different NA.
- Temperature coefficients depend on support: graphene 2D -0.034 cm-1/K supported vs -0.072 suspended
  (Calizo 2007, arXiv 0708.1223, Table I; Chen et al. via Lee et al. 2011, arXiv 1103.3337, p.2). Do not
  convert a shift into a temperature with a coefficient from a different geometry.
- Optothermal estimates need a peak-vs-T calibration, the absorbed (not incident) power, and a measured spot
  size; using two spot sizes helps (Malekpour and Balandin 2018, J. Raman Spectrosc. 49, 106; arXiv
  1710.09749, pp.4, 18).
- Stokes/anti-Stokes thermometry fails under resonance when incident and scattered windows differ (Ferrari
  and Basko 2013, Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 235; arXiv 1306.5856, p.12).
- Photodamage is dose-dependent: BP oxidation rate scales with fluence (Favron et al. 2015, arXiv 1408.0345,
  p.7); MnPS3 degraded at about 50 uW when one spot was illuminated 500 s or longer (Lim et al. 2021, Curr.
  Appl. Phys. 21, 1; doi 10.1016/j.cap.2020.09.017, pp.6-7, via Lit-RAG). Irreversible change in a repeat
  spectrum means damage, reversible shift means heating.

- A tightly focused beam has longitudinal (out-of-plane) field components that can excite modes forbidden for
  purely in-plane fields (Grosche et al. 2020, Opt. Express, doi 10.1364/OE.388943; arXiv 1905.12325,
  abstract). How large this leakage is for a standard 100x/0.9 objective was not quantified in what I read.
  [magnitude not verified]
- In birefringent crystals the classical Raman tensor fails because polarization changes with depth; an
  effective tensor is needed (Kranert et al. 2016, PRL 116, 127401, abstract). In thin anisotropic flakes on
  SiO2/Si, anisotropic interference changes polar patterns with thickness (Kim et al. 2015, arXiv 1510.03263).
- Si substrate intensity depends on Si crystal orientation to the laser polarization (Castellanos-Gomez 2014,
  p.8): sample/Si intensity ratios need fixed sample rotation.
- Ask whether the analyzer is fixed and a half-wave plate rotates the polarization, or the sample rotates;
  grating efficiency is polarization dependent [practice].

## Interference on SiO2/Si
- Graphene I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al. 2009, PRB 80,
  125422; arXiv 0908.4322, abstract, Fig. 2). Intensity ratios between bands at different shifts are
  stack-dependent.
- For MoS2 the sample intensity oscillates with thickness (interference maxima), but the ratio of sample to Si
  intensity becomes monotonic and gives thickness (Li et al. 2012, ACS Nano 6, 7381; arXiv 1308.3835,
  abstract, Fig. 4). Interference also changes optical contrast (Gorbachev et al. 2011, arXiv 1008.2868).

- hBN encapsulation narrows graphene 2D (16 to 20 vs above 22 cm-1 on SiO2) and changes doping (Neumann et
  al. 2015, arXiv 1406.7771, p.2); it narrows BP lines and reveals a surface mode (Urban et al., arXiv
  1711.08294, abstract). Compare encapsulated with encapsulated only.

  session, not absolute values across papers.

# Artifacts and red flags in Raman spectra of 2D materials

Each entry: what it looks like, how to tell it from a real band, what to do. Sources in brackets.

## Cosmic-ray spikes
- One to three pixels wide, far narrower than any phonon line at the instrument resolution, present in one
  acquisition only. Real lines have the instrument's minimum width and repeat across accumulations or angles.
- Remove before fitting (modified z-score on the first difference: Whitaker and Hayes, Chemom. Intell. Lab. Syst.
  179, 82, 2018). In an angle series, replace spike pixels from the most similar frame (Barton and Hennelly, Appl.
  Spectrosc. 73, 893, 2019). List them under artifacts, never under peaks.

## Silicon substrate
- First-order Si line near 520.7 cm-1 (a widely used calibration convention; check the offset of the fitted
  position and flag a calibration problem when it exceeds about 1 cm-1; 520 to 520.9 is reported in practice, Lee
  et al. 2010 and Castellanos-Gomez et al. 2014). Second-order Si features near 950 and 980 cm-1 (Gillet et al.
  2017, arXiv 1708.05874, Fig. 1) and a 2TA band computed near 300 cm-1 (same paper, DFPT) can be mistaken for
  sample modes. Brillouin scattering from Si gives a line near
  4.5 cm-1 in ultra-low-frequency setups (Zhang et al., PRB 87, 115413, 2013).
- Assign these as 'Si substrate'. A strong Si line with weak sample bands suggests a thin flake.

## Calibration
- First-order wavelength calibration errors of 5 to 7 cm-1 have been reported (Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1024,
  2012). Shifts of 1 to 3 cm-1 (layer number, strain, doping) are only meaningful after a calibration check.

## Background
- Broad fluorescence or photoluminescence slopes; remove with an asymmetric least-squares baseline (arPLS or
  asPLS). For broad bands (disordered carbon D and G, amorphous phases) a global baseline can eat real signal: fit
  a local linear background together with the peaks. A Breit-Wigner-Fano line shape can absorb a background slope;
  compare line shapes by BIC.

## Low-wavenumber cutoff
- Notch and edge filters block the region near the laser line (Bragg notch filters reach about 5 to 10 cm-1,
  Zhang et al. 2013). A missing shear or breathing mode below the cutoff is not evidence of absence.

## Plasma lines
- Laser plasma lines have a fixed absolute wavelength, so their Raman shift changes when the laser changes; they
  are very narrow and do not belong to the sample. Suspect them when a narrow line has no assignment.

## Laser heating
- Phonon lines soften and broaden with temperature. Graphene G shifts about -0.016 cm-1/K (Calizo et al., Nano
  Lett. 7, 2645, 2007); 1L WS2 about -0.0093 (E) and -0.0122 (A1g) cm-1/K (Huang et al., Sci. Rep. 2016);
  few-layer MoS2 about -0.013 and -0.012 cm-1/K (Sahoo et al., arXiv 1302.5865). A power series is the test.

## Substrate interference
- On SiO2/Si, absolute intensities and intensity ratios depend on oxide thickness and laser wavelength: graphene
  I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al., PRB 80, 125422, 2009).
  Never read layer number from absolute intensity or from I(2D)/I(G) without the substrate stack.

## Resonance
- Near an excitonic resonance, second-order bands can exceed first-order ones. WS2 at 514 to 532 nm: 2LA(M) lies
  about 4 cm-1 below E2g and overlaps it (Berkdemir et al., Sci. Rep. 3, 1755, 2013; Mitioglu et al., PRB 89,
  245442, 2014). Fit both or the E2g position and layer count are wrong.

## Saturation and clipping
- A flat-topped peak or values at the detector maximum: the peak shape and intensity are wrong; ask for a shorter
  exposure.

  SiO2/Si, anisotropic interference changes polar patterns with thickness (Kim et al. 2015, arXiv 1510.03263).
- Si substrate intensity depends on Si crystal orientation to the laser polarization (Castellanos-Gomez 2014,
  p.8): sample/Si intensity ratios need fixed sample rotation.
- Ask whether the analyzer is fixed and a half-wave plate rotates the polarization, or the sample rotates;
  grating efficiency is polarization dependent [practice].

## Interference on SiO2/Si
- Graphene I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al. 2009, PRB 80,
  125422; arXiv 0908.4322, abstract, Fig. 2). Intensity ratios between bands at different shifts are
  stack-dependent.
- For MoS2 the sample intensity oscillates with thickness (interference maxima), but the ratio of sample to Si
  intensity becomes monotonic and gives thickness (Li et al. 2012, ACS Nano 6, 7381; arXiv 1308.3835,
  abstract, Fig. 4). Interference also changes optical contrast (Gorbachev et al. 2011, arXiv 1008.2868).

## Encapsulation and overlayers
- hBN encapsulation narrows graphene 2D (16 to 20 vs above 22 cm-1 on SiO2) and changes doping (Neumann et
  al. 2015, arXiv 1406.7771, p.2); it narrows BP lines and reveals a surface mode (Urban et al., arXiv
  1711.08294, abstract). Compare encapsulated with encapsulated only.
- Overlayer lines can overlap sample lines: hBN E2g near 1366 cm-1 on graphene D (Purdie et al. 2018, Nat.
  Commun. 9, 5387, p.6, via Lit-RAG). Measure an overlayer-only reference spot.

## Low-frequency modes and filters
- Shear and breathing modes (tens of cm-1) need notch or Bragg filters reaching about 5 to 10 cm-1 and
  plasma-line cleanup (Zhang 2013, p.2). Many production spectrometers cut above the graphene C mode, so absence
  below the cutoff is not evidence (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.2). Odd and even layer numbers scale differently
  (Zhang 2013, abstract).

## Spikes, plasma lines, fluorescence, baseline
- Spikes and plasma lines: see ../artifacts.md (sources listed there, not re-verified here).
- Fluorescence or PL backgrounds: fit a local background with the peaks for broad bands; a global baseline can
  remove real broad signal [practice; see ../artifacts.md].

## Fitting line shapes and over-fitting
- Report whether ratios use heights or areas: graphene defect relations use heights (Cancado 2011) and heights
  and areas diverge in stage 2 (Eckmann et al. 2012, arXiv 1207.2058, p.5).
- Number of components needs physics: 1L graphene 2D one, Bernal 2L four (Ferrari 2006, p.2); unresolved
  doublets (BP Ag2 in few layers, resolved only at 77 K, Favron 2015, p.10) appear as broadening. Adding peaks
  without a physical reason fits noise; compare models by an information criterion [practice].
- Fit overlapping neighbours jointly (WS2 2LA(M) and E2g, see ../artifacts.md; hBN and graphene D, Purdie 2018).

## Comparing spectra from different setups
- Different lasers: dispersive bands (graphene D, 2D) move; resonances change relative intensities (Cancado
  2011; Kim et al. 2012, arXiv 1201.4221). Different spectrographs: calibration offsets of several cm-1 (Lee
  2012). Different substrates: interference changes ratios (Yoon 2009). Compare differences measured in one
  session, not absolute values across papers.

## Mapping statistics
- A spectrum averages over the spot: sub-spot strain variations show up as width, not shift (Neumann 2015,
  Fig. 1); mono- and bilayers can vary strongly from sample to sample (Gorbachev 2011, p.4).
- Use many points and correlations: hundreds of map pixels per sample fell on a G-2D line of slope 2.2 (Lee
  2012, p.3, Fig. 2). Report distributions (histograms, median and spread), not one "representative" spectrum.
- Move the spot between acquisitions on sensitive materials (Lim 2021).

## What to ask
- Laser line and power at sample, objective NA, spot size; grating, resolution, calibration lines and date.
- Substrate stack and oxide thickness; encapsulation; suspended or supported.
- Polarization geometry; temperature and atmosphere; exposure time; number of spectra and map size.

## Reference figures
- Yoon 2009, arXiv 0908.4322, Fig. 2: G and 2D intensities and their ratio vs SiO2 thickness.
- Li 2012, arXiv 1308.3835, Fig. 4: MoS2/Si intensity ratios vs layer number, calculated and measured.
- Zhang 2013, arXiv 1212.6796, Fig. 4: shear and breathing positions vs layer number (odd vs even).
- Neumann 2015, arXiv 1406.7771, Fig. 1: maps and 2D-width histograms, hBN vs SiO2 support.

# Artifacts and red flags in Raman spectra of 2D materials

Each entry: what it looks like, how to tell it from a real band, what to do. Sources in brackets.

## Cosmic-ray spikes
- One to three pixels wide, far narrower than any phonon line at the instrument resolution, present in one
  acquisition only. Real lines have the instrument's minimum width and repeat across accumulations or angles.
- Remove before fitting (modified z-score on the first difference: Whitaker and Hayes, Chemom. Intell. Lab. Syst.
  179, 82, 2018). In an angle series, replace spike pixels from the most similar frame (Barton and Hennelly, Appl.
  Spectrosc. 73, 893, 2019). List them under artifacts, never under peaks.

## Silicon substrate
- First-order Si line near 520.7 cm-1 (a widely used calibration convention; check the offset of the fitted
  position and flag a calibration problem when it exceeds about 1 cm-1; 520 to 520.9 is reported in practice, Lee
  et al. 2010 and Castellanos-Gomez et al. 2014). Second-order Si features near 950 and 980 cm-1 (Gillet et al.
  2017, arXiv 1708.05874, Fig. 1) and a 2TA band computed near 300 cm-1 (same paper, DFPT) can be mistaken for
  sample modes. Brillouin scattering from Si gives a line near
  4.5 cm-1 in ultra-low-frequency setups (Zhang et al., PRB 87, 115413, 2013).
- Assign these as 'Si substrate'. A strong Si line with weak sample bands suggests a thin flake.

## Calibration
- First-order wavelength calibration errors of 5 to 7 cm-1 have been reported (Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1024,
  2012). Shifts of 1 to 3 cm-1 (layer number, strain, doping) are only meaningful after a calibration check.

## Background
- Broad fluorescence or photoluminescence slopes; remove with an asymmetric least-squares baseline (arPLS or
  asPLS). For broad bands (disordered carbon D and G, amorphous phases) a global baseline can eat real signal: fit
  a local linear background together with the peaks. A Breit-Wigner-Fano line shape can absorb a background slope;
  compare line shapes by BIC.

## Low-wavenumber cutoff
- Notch and edge filters block the region near the laser line (Bragg notch filters reach about 5 to 10 cm-1,
  Zhang et al. 2013). A missing shear or breathing mode below the cutoff is not evidence of absence.

## Plasma lines
- Laser plasma lines have a fixed absolute wavelength, so their Raman shift changes when the laser changes; they
  are very narrow and do not belong to the sample. Suspect them when a narrow line has no assignment.

## Laser heating
- Phonon lines soften and broaden with temperature. Graphene G shifts about -0.016 cm-1/K (Calizo et al., Nano
  Lett. 7, 2645, 2007); 1L WS2 about -0.0093 (E) and -0.0122 (A1g) cm-1/K (Huang et al., Sci. Rep. 2016);
  few-layer MoS2 about -0.013 and -0.012 cm-1/K (Sahoo et al., arXiv 1302.5865). A power series is the test.

## Substrate interference
- On SiO2/Si, absolute intensities and intensity ratios depend on oxide thickness and laser wavelength: graphene
  I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al., PRB 80, 125422, 2009).
  Never read layer number from absolute intensity or from I(2D)/I(G) without the substrate stack.

## Resonance
- Near an excitonic resonance, second-order bands can exceed first-order ones. WS2 at 514 to 532 nm: 2LA(M) lies
  about 4 cm-1 below E2g and overlaps it (Berkdemir et al., Sci. Rep. 3, 1755, 2013; Mitioglu et al., PRB 89,
  245442, 2014). Fit both or the E2g position and layer count are wrong.

## Saturation and clipping
- A flat-topped peak or values at the detector maximum: the peak shape and intensity are wrong; ask for a shorter
  exposure.

C and E show no sharp Ag1 line at all, and D's Ag2 triplet is over-fitted. I'll refit the Ag1 and Ag2 regions in narrow windows so each flake's line positions don't depend on the broad low-frequency features.

input.summary: All six flakes show the same CrSBr fingerprint: three Ag modes near 108–114 (Ag1), 238–244 (Ag2) and 340–343 cm-1 (Ag3), with no sample Si line in the measured window. The flakes differ mainly in line widths, whether Ag1 is resolved at all, and raw Ag3 counts (about 8x range). Thickness is not measured here: no layer-number relation for CrSBr is in the library, and no AFM yet. Tentative thin-to-thick order, low confidence: A (most red-shifted Ag1, separated from the rest) < F ≈ D ≈ B (cluster, order not robust). C and E cannot be placed: no resolved Ag1, broad lines, and a broad hump near 103 cm-1. The AFM and a polarization check are needed before any thickness statement.

observations.finding: All six spectra contain the CrSBr Ag triplet (Ag1, Ag2, Ag3); identity is consistent with the reference set. Narrow-window single-Lorentzian fits: Ag1 A 108.58±0.04, B 114.03±0.04, D 113.31±0.03, F 111.93±0.05 cm-1; Ag2 A 241.49±0.08, B 244.42±0.04, D 243.94±0.06, F 242.69±0.09 cm-1; Ag3 A 341.12±0.03, B 342.89±0.03, D 342.07±0.03, F 340.56±0.04 cm-1.
observations.evidence: rl_fit.py with --window 95 130 (Ag1), 225 262 (Ag2), 328 356 (Ag3) on spectrum_A..F.csv; Ag1 FWHM 3.9-4.6 cm-1 in B, D, F and 7.0 in A. Reference: Mondal et al. 2025 (arXiv 2410.22164, p.2): 4L at 2.33 eV Ag1 114, Ag2 244, Ag3 344 cm-1; Pawbake et al. 2023 (arXiv 2211.12939, p.3): bulk 633 nm Ag1 117, Ag2 257, Ag3 345.

observations.finding: C and E have no resolved Ag1 line. The only feature in the 95-130 window is a broad Lorentzian at 103.42 cm-1 (FWHM 9.9 in C, 11.0 in E), roughly 2-3x wider than the Ag1 lines in B, D, F. Ag2 is also broad (8.1 and 7.8 cm-1) and shifted down to 238.3 and 238.7 cm-1. Ag3 is at 340.8 (C) and 340.2 (E).
observations.evidence: rl_fit windowed fits on C and E; visual check of fit_C/fit.png and series.png: no sharp peak near 110-115 cm-1 in C or E.

observations.finding: Ag1 spread across the set is 5.44 cm-1 (A to B), comparable to the 1L-to-bulk Ag1 span in Torres et al. (about 107 vs 113 cm-1, read from Fig. 1h, +-1 cm-1). Ag1 redshifts as layer number decreases, but the source gives only the direction and an approximate magnitude, measured with 1.58 eV resonant excitation rather than 2.33 eV.
observations.evidence: Ag1 positions from the window fits above; Ag1 minus Ag3 separation A 232.54, B 228.86, D 228.76, F 228.63 cm-1 (fit errors about 0.05 cm-1). Ag1 minus Ag3 cancels a rigid calibration offset, so A is the outlier in the calibration-free measure.
observations.source: Torres et al. 2022 (arXiv 2212.01754, Fig. 1h, read from plot, p.3); Ye et al. 2022 (ACS Nano 16, 11876, doi:10.1021/acsnano.2c01151, corpus p.6) for the same downshift trend.

observations.finding: Ag3 is nearly layer-independent in the literature, but here it spans 340.17 to 342.89 cm-1 (2.7 cm-1) across the six flakes at identical settings. That scatter is larger than the fit errors and points to calibration drift between acquisitions, flake-to-flake strain, or spot differences rather than thickness. No Si reference is in the measured window to check it.
observations.evidence: Ag3 positions above; QC si_line null (window 50.8-430.8 cm-1, Si 520 cm-1 outside it); rl_series --si-correct made no correction (notes: no Si line found for all six).

observations.finding: Flake B matches the 4-layer reference at 2.33 eV on 85 nm SiO2/Si (Ag1 114.0 vs 114, Ag2 244.4 vs 244, Ag3 342.9 vs 344). This is a consistency check, not a layer number: the match is within the calibration scatter, and Ag1 also changes with laser energy and substrate.
observations.evidence: B window fits vs Mondal et al. 2025 p.2 values.

observations.finding: Line widths separate the set: B and D are sharpest (Ag3 FWHM 4.1 and 4.6 cm-1), F intermediate (5.5), A broader (6.8), and C and E broadest (7.1 and 7.0). Raw Ag3 counts vary about 8x (B 2.3k, C 1.2k, E 3.5k, D 10.5k, A 13.5k, F 18.0k) at identical settings, so counts do not map to thickness.
observations.evidence: Ag3 window fits: FWHM and height; point spacing is 1.22 cm-1, so FWHM near 4 cm-1 is only about 3 points and may be instrument-limited (resolution not supplied).

observations.finding: A weak band near 301-302 cm-1 appears in A, C, E and F but not in B or D. In normal-incidence backscattering the 301 cm-1 B2g mode should be absent: it appears only in a 60-degree tilted sample, per Pawbake et al. 2023 (p.3, Fig. 1c). Its presence needs an explanation, such as objective NA leakage, a tilted or wrinkled flake, or Si 2TA; it is not a thickness marker.
observations.evidence: Full-window fits: 302.3 cm-1 (C, FWHM 11.0, height 238), 302.1 (E, FWHM 12.2, height 720), 301.6 (A, height 435), 301.2 (F, height 189); none resolved in B or D.
observations.source: Pawbake et al. 2023 (arXiv 2211.12939, p.3, Fig. 1c); Grosche et al. 2020 (Opt. Express, doi 10.1364/OE.388943, via general-measurement note) for NA leakage.

observations.finding: The steep rise between about 65 and 80 cm-1 in every spectrum looks like the low-wavenumber edge filter. The broad humps at 85 cm-1 (A, F) and about 100 cm-1 (C, E) sit on that edge, so they cannot yet be assigned to a sample mode. For C and E, the 103 cm-1 hump is 8-10 cm-1 below the expected Ag1 position, which is where a D1 defect shoulder would sit (Torres 2022 p.4-5), but a filter-edge or background explanation is equally possible.
observations.evidence: Raw spectra in series.png; fit_F residual of about -4000 counts at 50-110 cm-1 from the broad-Lorentzian fit; fit_D residual positive at 70-180 cm-1.
observations.source: reference/artifacts.md (low-wavenumber cutoff); Torres et al. 2022 (arXiv 2212.01754, p.4-5) for D1.

observations.finding: D shows a 1.7 cm-1 doublet in its full-window Ag3 fit (341.48 and 343.21 cm-1) and an over-fitted Ag2 triplet (241.7, 243.5, 245.3 cm-1 with errors up to 4 cm-1). A single-Lorentzian refit gives Ag2 243.94 and Ag3 342.07, but the residual still shows structure at the top of Ag3, so a real doublet (two domains or a strain gradient within the spot) is possible.
observations.evidence: fit_D/fit.png and win_ag3_D/fit.png residuals; the window fit is 342.07 with FWHM 4.6 and a systematic of about 0.8 cm-1 from the doublet ambiguity.

caveats: Absolute layer number cannot come from these data. The only validated CrSBr thickness trend in the notes is qualitative (Ag1 and Ag2 redshift as layers are removed, Ag3 flat), and the quantitative Ag1 magnitude comes from a 1.58 eV resonant plot read to about 1 cm-1. Optical contrast or AFM is the right method (Ye 2022, corpus p.5). The AFM you have not analysed yet is the decisive check.

The substrate was not stated. I assumed SiO2/Si (the note's reference substrate is 85 nm SiO2/Si; your 'marked substrate' may differ). Oxide thickness is unknown, so intensity ratios and absolute counts are interference-dependent and were not used for ranking.

No Si reference is inside the measured window (50.8-430.8 cm-1, so Si 520 cm-1 is excluded). The --si-correct flag therefore did nothing, and absolute positions carry an unknown calibration offset. Only differences between flakes measured in one session are meaningful, and even these carry a systematic of order a few tenths to about 1 cm-1 (Lee et al. 2012, Nat. Commun. 3, 1024, Methods p.10).

The Ag1 and Ag2 positions differ between literature sources by several cm-1 (Ag2 244 at 4L, 2.33 eV, vs 257 for bulk at 633 nm; Pawbake 2023 vs Mondal 2025), and Ag2 also switches with laser energy and crystal axis. Ag2 is therefore a weaker thickness marker here than Ag1, and I did not use Ag2 to set the ranking beyond a consistency check.

Polarization geometry is unknown. Ag1 and Ag3 are maximal with E parallel to b, and Ag2 is maximal along a at 2.33 eV (Mondal 2025). If C and E sit with b perpendicular to the laser polarization, Ag1 and Ag3 would be suppressed without any thickness change, which may explain their weak Ag1 and low counts. An angle series on C and E would separate orientation from thickness or quality.

The spectral sampling is 1.22 cm-1 per point and the instrument resolution was not supplied. FWHM values near 4 cm-1 (B, D) are only about 3 points wide and may be partly instrument-limited, so width differences of about 1 cm-1 are not significant.

Only the 50-431 cm-1 window was measured. Second-order bands (370-780 cm-1, which Pawbake 2023 reports below about 160 K), the D3 region near 350 cm-1, and the Si 520 line were not checked. Absence in this window is not evidence of absence.

Laser power density, spot size, numerical aperture and exposure time were not given. Laser heating and photodamage cannot be excluded. A power series on one flake would test heating (Ag3 and Ag1 softening) and damage (irreversible change), per the general-measurement note.

The fit scripts wrote output into the data folder: series.png, and fit_A to fit_F and win_ag1_*, win_ag2_*, win_ag3_* subfolders with fit.png and peaks.json. Delete them if you do not want them there.

Ag3 is the only mode the literature says is nearly thickness-independent, so its 2.7 cm-1 scatter is my main evidence that calibration or flake-to-flake strain differs between the six acquisitions. This has not been checked against a Si or Ne reference.
questions_for_user: AFM heights for flakes A to F. This is the only route to layer number. The Raman ordering here is a hypothesis to test against it, and it is not yet a thickness result.

Did you acquire a Si reference in the same session, and can you extend the spectra to about 600 cm-1? That gives a calibration offset for Ag3 and a Si-normalised intensity, and brings the second-order region into view.
What substrate and oxide thickness did you use? Interference on SiO2/Si changes absolute counts by large factors (Yoon et al. 2009, PRB 80, 125422), so counts cannot rank the flakes without it.

What is the laser polarization relative to the flake's long edge (a axis) and what was the orientation of each flake? An angle series on C and E would show whether their weak Ag1 and Ag3 is orientation or thickness.

How long were the flakes exposed to air between exfoliation or transfer and measurement? Thin CrSBr degrades in air, and the broad, Ag1-depleted spectra in C and E could be degradation (Torres 2022, p.4-5).

What is the instrument resolution (Rayleigh line width at 532 nm) and the power density at the sample? These decide whether B and D's 4 cm-1 widths are real and whether heating is a concern at 200 uW.
Were all six spectra taken from one spot per flake, and in what order? Acquisition order and drift would explain part of the 2.7 cm-1 Ag3 scatter.

limits: Thickness of each flake is not determined. The ranking is a tentative ordering from Ag1 position and Ag1-Ag3 separation, not a layer count.
The ordering among B, D and F (Ag1 111.9 to 114.0 cm-1) is within the plausible calibration scatter (Ag3 spread 2.7 cm-1) and is not robust.

C and E could not be placed: no resolved Ag1 line and broad Ag2. Their broad lines and missing Ag1 are consistent with thin or degraded flakes, with orientation effects, or with a filter-edge artifact, and the data alone cannot pick one.
The relation library has no validated layer-number relation for CrSBr. The only applicable relation (mode-axis assignment) needs an angle series, which was not measured, so it was not applied.

No polarization data, no Si or other calibration reference, no substrate thickness, no AFM, no power density and no resolution figure were supplied. Each limits the thickness and calibration statements above.
Mode assignments use the curated CrSBr reference set (Ag1, Ag2, Ag3). B2g assignments are excluded for normal incidence. The 302 cm-1 band is flagged as unexplained rather than assigned.

caveats: Absolute layer number cannot come from these data. The only validated CrSBr thickness trend in the notes is qualitative (Ag1 and Ag2 redshift as layers are removed, Ag3 flat), and the quantitative Ag1 magnitude comes from a 1.58 eV resonant plot read to about 1 cm-1. Optical contrast or AFM is the right method (Ye 2022, corpus p.5). The AFM you have not analysed yet is the decisive check.

The substrate was not stated. I assumed SiO2/Si (the note's reference substrate is 85 nm SiO2/Si; your 'marked substrate' may differ). Oxide thickness is unknown, so intensity ratios and absolute counts are interference-dependent and were not used for ranking.

No Si reference is inside the measured window (50.8-430.8 cm-1, so Si 520 cm-1 is excluded). The --si-correct flag therefore did nothing, and absolute positions carry an unknown calibration offset. Only differences between flakes measured in one session are meaningful, and even these carry a systematic of order a few tenths to about 1 cm-1 (Lee et al. 2012, Nat. Commun. 3, 1024, Methods p.10).

The Ag1 and Ag2 positions differ between literature sources by several cm-1 (Ag2 244 at 4L, 2.33 eV, vs 257 for bulk at 633 nm; Pawbake 2023 vs Mondal 2025), and Ag2 also switches with laser energy and crystal axis. Ag2 is therefore a weaker thickness marker here than Ag1, and I did not use Ag2 to set the ranking beyond a consistency check.

Polarization geometry is unknown. Ag1 and Ag3 are maximal with E parallel to b, and Ag2 is maximal along a at 2.33 eV (Mondal 2025). If C and E sit with b perpendicular to the laser polarization, Ag1 and Ag3 would be suppressed without any thickness change, which may explain their weak Ag1 and low counts. An angle series on C and E would separate orientation from thickness or quality.

The spectral sampling is 1.22 cm-1 per point and the instrument resolution was not supplied. FWHM values near 4 cm-1 (B, D) are only about 3 points wide and may be partly instrument-limited, so width differences of about 1 cm-1 are not significant.

Only the 50-431 cm-1 window was measured. Second-order bands (370-780 cm-1, which Pawbake 2023 reports below about 160 K), the D3 region near 350 cm-1, and the Si 520 line were not checked. Absence in this window is not evidence of absence.

Laser power density, spot size, numerical aperture and exposure time were not given. Laser heating and photodamage cannot be excluded. A power series on one flake would test heating (Ag3 and Ag1 softening) and damage (irreversible change), per the general-measurement note.

The fit scripts wrote output into the data folder: series.png, and fit_A to fit_F and win_ag1_*, win_ag2_*, win_ag3_* subfolders with fit.png and peaks.json. Delete them if you do not want them there.

Ag3 is the only mode the literature says is nearly thickness-independent, so its 2.7 cm-1 scatter is my main evidence that calibration or flake-to-flake strain differs between the six acquisitions. This has not been checked against a Si or Ne reference.
questions_for_user: AFM heights for flakes A to F. This is the only route to layer number. The Raman ordering here is a hypothesis to test against it, and it is not yet a thickness result.

Did you acquire a Si reference in the same session, and can you extend the spectra to about 600 cm-1? That gives a calibration offset for Ag3 and a Si-normalised intensity, and brings the second-order region into view.
What substrate and oxide thickness did you use? Interference on SiO2/Si changes absolute counts by large factors (Yoon et al. 2009, PRB 80, 125422), so counts cannot rank the flakes without it.

What is the laser polarization relative to the flake's long edge (a axis) and what was the orientation of each flake? An angle series on C and E would show whether their weak Ag1 and Ag3 is orientation or thickness.

How long were the flakes exposed to air between exfoliation or transfer and measurement? Thin CrSBr degrades in air, and the broad, Ag1-depleted spectra in C and E could be degradation (Torres 2022, p.4-5).

What is the instrument resolution (Rayleigh line width at 532 nm) and the power density at the sample? These decide whether B and D's 4 cm-1 widths are real and whether heating is a concern at 200 uW.
Were all six spectra taken from one spot per flake, and in what order? Acquisition order and drift would explain part of the 2.7 cm-1 Ag3 scatter.

limits: Thickness of each flake is not determined. The ranking is a tentative ordering from Ag1 position and Ag1-Ag3 separation, not a layer count.
The ordering among B, D and F (Ag1 111.9 to 114.0 cm-1) is within the plausible calibration scatter (Ag3 spread 2.7 cm-1) and is not robust.

C and E could not be placed: no resolved Ag1 line and broad Ag2. Their broad lines and missing Ag1 are consistent with thin or degraded flakes, with orientation effects, or with a filter-edge artifact, and the data alone cannot pick one.
The relation library has no validated layer-number relation for CrSBr. The only applicable relation (mode-axis assignment) needs an angle series, which was not measured, so it was not applied.

No polarization data, no Si or other calibration reference, no substrate thickness, no AFM, no power density and no resolution figure were supplied. Each limits the thickness and calibration statements above.
Mode assignments use the curated CrSBr reference set (Ag1, Ag2, Ag3). B2g assignments are excluded for normal incidence. The 302 cm-1 band is flagged as unexplained rather than assigned.
